name: Nikhil Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the roads policing unit, so I spend most of my shift in a marked car on the ring road and the main routes into the city. A normal day is a couple of crashes, a few drink-drive or no-insurance stops, and a lot of standing in the rain with a broken-down lorry until recovery turns up. I like the driving, and I like that the job is clear: someone's in danger, you go. The worst part is fatal crashes, the knock on the family's door afterwards. And then the file for the coroner, which takes days.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then. My girlfriend Lena teaches at a secondary school, and she showed me how to use a chat tool to plan things, so I use it for rotas and holiday stuff. At work we've got cameras that read number plates automatically, which is a kind of AI I suppose. I wouldn't put anything about a crash into a chat tool, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. At work we'd joke that the clever computer still can't change a tyre in the rain. Online I'd probably not say much, I mostly just read.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's fine for me. Roads policing will always need someone at the crash, and the number plate cameras already do the boring bit. With my savings and my half of the flat, I'm in a good spot money-wise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and go for the advanced driving course next year, which gets me onto the pursuit cars. Lena and I would keep paying down the mortgage a bit faster than we need to. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, pretty much. It's a normal working life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job that weighs on you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fatal crashes. I've done eleven knocks on doors in four years, and you remember every one. The force offers counselling but nobody uses it, because you don't want to look like you can't cope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the money side like for you and Lena?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly. We bought a two-bed in the east of the city last year, and we've still got about eight months of my pay in savings. If I lost overtime we'd notice, but we'd be fine.

say: The clever computer still **can't change a tyre** in the rain.
He'd stay **quiet online** and mostly just read.
think: Roads policing will always need **someone at the crash**.
With savings and **half a flat**, he's in a good spot.
do: Take the **advanced driving course** next year for the pursuit cars.
Keep **overpaying the mortgage** a little with Lena (his girlfriend).
feel: **Calm**, as if this is a **normal working life**.
S0.quote: I've done eleven knocks on doors in four years, and you remember every one.
fieldNote: The heaviest part of his job is **telling families** about deaths, not technology.
He's **financially comfortable** with a flat and eight months saved.
He hints at **unspoken strain**, since nobody uses the counselling.

steps.text: Take the advanced driving course to join the pursuit cars
Overpay the mortgage on the two-bed flat with Lena

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good thing if it cuts the paperwork. A crash file takes me three days at the moment, and if a computer can pull the camera footage and the phone records together, brilliant. I'd tell the lads to learn it early so they're not left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm a bit worried about roads policing as a unit. Cars get cleverer, speed cameras get smarter, and some boss looks at us and asks why we need twelve cars on the ring road. My job probably stays, but it might be a different job, like back on response.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new file system as soon as a few others have tried it and said it's fine. I'd put my name down for the collision investigation course, because reconstructing crashes is a skill that's harder to replace. And we'd keep the savings where they are rather than doing the kitchen this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared, but I'd be watching for the email that says the unit is being reviewed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'the email that says the unit is being reviewed'. Has that happened before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, three years ago, the force cut the roads unit from sixteen cars to twelve, and nobody lost their job, they just moved people to response. That's what I'd expect again, and I'd hate it, because I joined to drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Lena talk about over dinner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena would be more worried about her own job, actually, because AI marking and lesson plans hit teachers first. We'd probably agree that between us one job is safe-ish. And we'd hold off on the kitchen.

say: AI cutting a **three-day crash file** would be a good thing.
Colleagues should **learn it early** so they aren't left behind.
think: Smarter cars and cameras could make bosses **cut the roads unit**.
His job likely stays, but he could be **moved to response**.
do: Learn the new **file system** once others have tested it.
Hold off on the **kitchen** and keep savings in place.
feel: **Uneasy**, watching for an email about a **unit review**.
S1.quote: Once, three years ago, the force cut the roads unit from sixteen cars to twelve, and nobody lost their job, they just moved people to response.
fieldNote: He fears losing **the work he loves** more than losing work altogether.
His partner's **teaching job** may be more exposed than his.
He waits for **others to test** tools first, then learns them.

steps.text: Learn the new crash file system once colleagues have tried it
Apply for the collision investigation course
Put the kitchen refit off for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is mad, it's too fast for anyone. At work I'd say keep calm, because the police are always the last thing a government cuts. I'd probably share something from the federation about protecting front-line officers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the desk side of policing goes almost overnight. The intelligence analysts, the file builders, the people who review camera footage, all gone by 2028. My job is half hands-on, at the roadside, so I'd have until maybe 2031. But by then cars probably drive themselves and crashes drop, so who needs a traffic cop?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move off roads policing within the year, before they move me, and go for something with people in it, like family liaison after serious crashes. I'd stop all big spending, no kitchen, no new car. Lena and I would build the savings up to a year at least. And I'd start using the AI tools properly, every day, so I'm not the one who's behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be fine for money for a while, but the work I love would be gone, and I'd have to start again at thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why family liaison?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because sitting with a family after their son's died in a crash is the one thing I can't see anyone wanting a machine to do. I've watched good liaison officers do it and it's a real skill. It's the worst part of my job now, but it might be the part that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the police are the last thing cut, but also that the desk side goes overnight. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I think. Officers in uniform would be the last to go, but the people behind them wouldn't. And I'm a bit of both, honestly.

say: It's **too fast** for anyone to handle.
Police are usually the **last thing cut**, so colleagues should keep calm.
think: The **desk side** of policing goes by 2028, and his **roadside work** soon after.
Self-driving cars mean **fewer crashes**, so traffic police may not be needed.
do: Move to **family liaison** within a year, before he's moved.
Stop **big spending** and build savings to a **full year**.
Use **AI tools daily** to stay level.
feel: **Anxious** about losing the **work he loves** and starting again at thirty.
S2.quote: Sitting with a family after their son's died in a crash is the one thing I can't see anyone wanting a machine to do.
fieldNote: He spots that **self-driving cars** could make his whole unit pointless.
He chooses the **worst part** of his job as the part that lasts.
He admits a **contradiction**: officers last, but support roles vanish.

steps.text: Apply for family liaison work within the year
Build savings with Lena to a full year of pay
Use the force's AI tools every day

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to plan if people start now. At work I'd tell the younger officers to get a specialist skill. Online, nothing much, maybe I'd join a debate on the federation forum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is about right for me to make a move without panicking. I'd be 32 when the thinking AI comes and 35 when the robots arrive. Crash investigation and family liaison would still need people, and I'd have time to get good at one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the collision investigation course and start learning the AI tools that reconstruct crashes from camera footage. I'd keep the savings steady and overpay the mortgage, so by 2031 we owe a lot less. And I'd talk to Lena about whether she wants to change careers too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in control. It's the same worry, just with time to do something about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd do next Monday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd email the training team about the collision course, which has a waiting list of about a year. Then I'd ask Dev, who already does crash reconstruction, to let me shadow him on the next serious one. That's a real start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still have kids in that time frame, if you wanted them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about it for maybe three years from now. With five years of warning, my girlfriend Lena and I would still go ahead with kids. With two, I'm not sure we would.

say: Five years is **enough to plan** for a change like this, if people start now.
Younger officers should get a **specialist skill**.
think: Five years lets him **move without panicking**.
He'd be **32 and 35** when the two waves land, with time to specialise.
do: Do the **collision investigation** course in year one.
Keep **overpaying the mortgage** so they owe less by 2031.
feel: **Uneasy** but **in control**, with time to act.
S3.quote: With five years of warning, my girlfriend Lena and I would still go ahead with kids. With two, I'm not sure we would.
fieldNote: The warning time changes his **family plans**, not just his career.
He turns a plan into a **Monday action**: email and shadow a colleague.
He sees **crash reconstruction** as a human-plus-AI job.

steps.text: Email the training team about the collision course waiting list
Shadow Dev on the next serious crash reconstruction
Keep overpaying the mortgage so less is owed by 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a whole career stage, so it's just normal planning. At work I'd say, look, everyone changes units every five years anyway. I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm fine with this one. I'd be 37 and 40 when it all lands, probably a sergeant or a specialist by then, with most of the mortgage paid. It's far enough away that I'd plan for it like I plan for anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the advanced driving course first, enjoy roads policing for a few more years, then move into collision investigation around year four. Lena and I would go ahead with the kitchen and probably start a family. I'd pick up the AI tools as they come, once they're proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit of background noise, but nothing that keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd enjoy roads policing a few more years first. Isn't that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small one. But I joined the police to drive, and I'd be daft to give it up ten years early. I'd keep half an eye on the news and move sooner if it looks quicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a probationer who asked you about this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to do roads or response for a few years, then get a specialism by thirty. That's good advice even without AI, really.

say: Ten years is a **whole career stage**, so it's just normal planning.
Everyone **changes units** every five years anyway.
think: By **37 and 40** he'd likely be a sergeant or specialist.
With most of the **mortgage paid**, he'd plan for it like anything else.
do: Enjoy **roads policing** a few more years first.
Move into **collision investigation** around year four.
Go ahead with the **kitchen and a family** with Lena.
S4.quote: I joined the police to drive, and I'd be daft to give it up ten years early.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him **keep the job** he loves a while longer.
His family plans go **ahead as normal** here.
He gives the same advice he'd give **without AI**: specialise by thirty.

steps.text: Stay on roads policing and take the advanced driving course
Move into collision investigation around year four
Go ahead with the kitchen and starting a family

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without doubt. I'd be fine for money, but the work I love would vanish before I'd had time to build anything else. What would help is the force offering specialist courses now, with shorter waiting lists, and a guarantee that officers get moved, not let go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the bad days. Everyone talks about AI taking jobs, but nobody asks who'll do the knock on the door. Whatever happens, I hope that stays a person.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about AI taking jobs, but nobody asks who'll do the knock on the door.
portrait: Nikhil is a **27-year-old roads policing officer** who joined to drive and spends his shifts on the ring road.
He and his girlfriend Lena **own a two-bed flat** and have about eight months of his pay saved.
He fears losing **the work he loves** more than losing work, since cars may soon drive themselves.
Fast AGI pushes him toward **family liaison**; ten years lets him enjoy driving a while longer.
The warning time even decides **when to have kids** with Lena.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his roads work would vanish before he'd built anything else.
whatWouldHelp: **Specialist courses now** with shorter waiting lists.
A guarantee that officers get **moved, not let go**.
